newsitem.title: USA: U.S. aims to get Kurds to negotiating table.
newsitem.headline: U.S. aims to get Kurds to negotiating table.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday announced plans for a new diplomatic initiative with Iraqi Kurds, insisting it was not in the Kurds' long-term interest to remain allied with Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
The new effort seeks to bring Kurdish leader Massood Barzani back into negotiations with rival Jalal Talabani, whose forces were defeated by Barzani with Saddam's assistance two weeks ago.

Toward this end, Assistant Secretary of State Robert Pelletreau is expected to meet Barzani on Thursday and it is hoped talks with Talabani can also be arranged in the future, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
"Our objective is to have Mr. Barzani and Mr. Talabani agree to talk about their differences peacefully and across from one another at the negotiating table," Burns said.

"The meeting on Thursday (between Barzani and Pelletreau) will not be a trilateral meeting ... We do hope it will be possible for the United States to arrange a meeting with Mr. Talabani in the future," he told reporters.

U.S. officials for several years had been working to bring the two main Kurdish factions in northern Iraq into political reconciliation. But talks broke down on Aug. 30 and the two sides resumed fighting, with Barzani winning control of the region with the assistance of Iraqi forces.
The United States then launched air strikes against targets in southern Iraq to curb further moves by Saddam.
Burns said Washington resumed its diplomatic activity after receiving a letter from Barzani more than one week ago.
He said it was uncertain where the Barzani-Pelletreau meeting would take place, but an Iraqi opposition group reported the venue would be Turkey.
Burns said Pelletreau had a "detailed agenda" to discuss with Barzani, but refused to lay it out publicly.

"The United States will repeat our very deeply held concerns about the situation in northern Iraq, about the lack of stability caused by the fighting, about our concern for Kurds and other ethnic groups in northern Iraq and about the humanitarian situation in northern Iraq," Burns said.

Pelletreau will "repeat the advice privately that we have tried to give Mr. Barzani and Mr. Talabani in public ... that Mr. Barzani's relationship with Saddam Hussein cannot be in the long term interest of his people or himself," he said.
The United States wants Barzani to end his alliance from Saddam and Talabani to end his ties with Iran.

Barzani told Reuters in Ankara: "We do not have any other deals with (Saddam) and that is really our message to the Americans." A U.S. official, asked how Washington could again trust Barzani, said: "It's not a question of trust."

Barzani's alliance with Saddam not only allowed his forces to defeat Talabani. The conflict and subsequent U.S. air strikes also forced a hasty end to U.S. programs in northern Iraq that supported dissident Kurds in efforts to overthrow Saddam and provided Kurds with humanitarian aid.
Burns argued that Washington did not fail in its endeavor to bring the Kurdish factions into a negotiated settlement.
"If there's any responsibility here, it's with the two Kurdish groups for the outbreak of this fighting, not with the United States," he said.

"...over the last five years, we kept our commitments... We protected them, we gave them humanitarian food and medical assistance. We saved them in March of 1991 from Saddam Hussein (who tried to) exterminate them," he said.

"It was not a lack of money that led to the outbreak of fighting between the two Kurdish factions. It was their own inclinations and their own tactics, and we very much disagree with their choice to fight rather than to continue to negotiate," he added.

Burns announced that the first two planes transporting a total of 2,080 Iraqis who worked for the United States in northern Iraq had arrived on the Pacific island of Guam enroute to new lives in America to escape Saddam's grasp.
